rows.text: TET-28's "workspace-rooted" requirement is NOT decidable from today's capture in the case that matters most. When look_grep finds matches, it records one extent entry per matched file, keyed on that file's resolved path, with label "<file> (grep: <pattern>)" — and the search root appears nowhere in what is captured; the code's own comment says the entries are keyed "not by the search root or the grep command line". A repo-wide grep and a single-file grep that matched the same file therefore capture byte-identical extents. Every genuine census of a symbol an implementer is told to modify falls in this positive-match case, because the symbol's definition site matches.

rows.text: A census check cannot be built on labels, and the record model already shows the right way to extend the schema. At mint time only key, label, world_root and world_state survive into an ExtentEntry — the observation's kind is dropped, and the grep pattern exists only inside a display label, where an author-chosen pattern containing " in " or "(grep: " would make parsing ambiguous. The census therefore needs the new root-level search entry to carry two structured fields into ExtentEntry — the observation kind and the search pattern — following the exact precedent world_root set: #[serde(default)], with the empty value read as "predates the field, not eligible" rather than guessed about. Legacy facts can then never satisfy a census requirement, whose remedy is precisely to re-run the grep under the new capture. The snapshot already ships facts.jsonl with full extent entries, so check reads these fields from files every snapshot already contains; and because no surface lets an author supply an extent by hand, both sides of the rooting comparison and the pattern are tool-captured by construction.

The charter forbids heuristic refusals outright, and scope.rs records the measurement: string-matching symbol references was tried for the note-outside-extent check and rejected because it "would have flagged a legitimate quotation ... while missing both real overreaches" — naming a symbol is normal, concluding about it is the failure, "and those two are not distinguishable by string matching". rows.text: The decidable trigger is declaration (candidate 1): a modification target is a structured record the author creates — a symbol string plus a fact citation — and the refusal fires only on a declared target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry. This sits inside the machine partition's own stated principle, that machine failures are "objective contradictions between a document and the record it claims to rest on, decidable without a human": a target row is exactly a pointer at evidence, and "you did not point at your evidence" is the README's own example of a decidable question. The refusal's remedy is singular — run the workspace-rooted grep for that symbol, mint the fact, cite it (or withdraw the target) — so refusal rather than report is the right disposition for the declared-but-uncensused case, by the same discriminator under which scope.rs chose report: there, only a person can tell context from conclusion; here, nothing is left to tell.

rows.text: Under-declaration — the memo recommends modifying a symbol it never declared — cannot be a refusal and must not be silently absorbed either. Deciding from prose that a sentence "tells an implementer to modify X" is a heuristic read of English, exactly the class the charter routes to the human-owed partition or nowhere; scope.rs's measured precedent shows the symbol-detector that trigger would need flags quotation and misses conclusion. The design therefore makes the omission visible instead of detected: (a) once a workspace declares any target, render emits a Modification targets section, and once any claim exists it emits the section even when empty — "Modification targets: none declared" — so a memo that recommends changes while declaring nothing shows a hole where the census should be, in front of every reader; and (b) check's standing non-coverage list, whose first entry is already "dependents that never declared themselves", gains a census-specific line ("a recommendation whose target was never declared") so the blind spot is printed rather than implicit.

rows.text: Where the refusal lives: at declaration, then re-verified at check. The `target` verb refuses to create a target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry — the same authoring-time shape as fact refusing on an empty pending buffer ("a fact needs a preceding look/run"; a target needs a preceding rooted census). Because a fact's extent is immutable once minted and a target is immutable once declared, this makes "every declared target is censused" a workspace invariant, and no render-path refusal is needed for workspace-authored documents; render's job is only to emit the targets section. check independently re-verifies the rendered document against its snapshot and reports [uncensused-target] as a machine failure in the partition's scope line, which is what catches a hand-authored or tampered document that never passed through the refusing verb. Like notes_outside_extent and mint_windows, that check runs only when a snapshot ships; without one, target rows are reported human-owed as unverifiable, consistent with the standing choice that a missing snapshot is human-owed rather than a machine failure. The verb must be one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, the pattern look and fact already use, because this codebase has recorded a CLI/MCP drift on exactly such a duplicated act.

rows.text: The rooting predicate — census entry's key byte-equals its own world_root — is satisfiable and fails closed. On this machine and repo the two spellings (fs-canonicalized search root; git rev-parse --show-toplevel) agree byte-for-byte, so an honestly rooted grep satisfies the predicate; and if the two tools ever disagree on spelling, the mismatch refuses an honest census loudly rather than accepting an unrooted one silently, because inequality can only ever deny rooting, never grant it. Two hardenings belong in the implementation: look_grep should itself compare the canonicalized search root against the marker's root at capture time and store the search entry's key in the marker's spelling when they name the same directory, so check stays a pure byte comparison; and the agreement should be pinned by a test, since one probe on one machine shows the common case, not an invariant.

rows.text: The qualifying-census predicate, fully: a declared target (symbol S, citing fact F) is censused iff F's captured extent contains a search entry whose kind field says it is a whole-search record, whose pattern field byte-equals S, whose key byte-equals its own world_root, and whose world_root is git-backed (neither the no-git sentinel nor the empty predates-the-field value). Byte-equality of pattern to symbol is the only sound decidable comparison available: grep is invoked with the pattern verbatim (-e <pattern>), so a looser rule like "pattern contains the symbol" would accept a grep whose pattern merely embeds S in a longer string and therefore matches a strict subset of S's textual occurrences, while anything semantically wider would require deciding containment between regular expressions. Symbols that are not literal strings in the system grep's dialect are a stated limit of the census, not a case the check adjudicates.

rows.text: The census's blind spots are boundable from what the capture actually does, and belong in check's printed non-coverage: (a) a textual grep cannot see dynamic dispatch, re-exports and aliased imports, or macro-generated and string-assembled identifiers; (b) the traversal is the system grep's — tetel deliberately shells out to it rather than reimplementing a dialect — so platform rules about symlinked directories and the -I binary skip bound what a "repo-wide" search physically visited; (c) rooting says where the search started, not which tree it should have been: whether the censused root is the tree the memo designs against stays with the reader, alongside the existing per-root tree-state report; (d) whether anyone read the census is the insincere-examination ceiling — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation; and (e) under-declared targets, by construction. The report mechanism for printing exactly this kind of standing limit already exists as the NON_COVERAGE list.

So a transplant is a record the author declares, the refusal attaches to the declaration, and under-declaration is handled the way TET-28 handles it: an always-rendered section that shows its hole, plus a printed non-coverage line, never a detector.

rows.text: "Transcribed verbatim" cannot be an honour-system field, and does not need to be: the decidable relation is that a premise's text is refused unless it is a verbatim substring of the cited donor fact's captured output. Both sides of that comparison are Strings the tool controls — a fact's output is produced only by look/run (file bytes read verbatim by look_path, grep match lines, a process's merged stream), no authoring surface lets anyone supply output by hand, and output is immutable after mint — so substring containment is a pure byte-level comparison with no normalisation step owned by the check. Typing is the selection mechanism, not the trust: the author types the premise, but a typed premise the donor never wrote fails containment and is refused at the verb. This is exactly the README's Direction item for supporting-span selection ("refused unless it is a verbatim substring of a cited fact — the author cannot type an extent, and here could not invent support, only select it"), and TET-29 is the first place it becomes load-bearing rather than roadmap.

rows.text: The strictness objections to byte-level containment dissolve on the actual capture path, and every weaker relation reopens the invention channel. A donor comment wrapped across lines with interior prefix noise (`//`, `*`, indentation) IS a contiguous byte substring of a look_path capture, because look_path stores the file's bytes verbatim — the cost is only that the selected premise carries its comment syntax into the rendered section, which the "never paraphrase" constraint endorses rather than tolerates. Stripping that noise would require knowing each language's comment syntax, which is precisely the hard-coded per-language coupling scope.rs's "language-agnostic by construction" doctrine excludes. Two capture modes genuinely fight containment — grep-derived match outputs interleave "lineno:" prefixes between lines, and whole-search/no-match records carry empty output — so the design's guidance is that a donor fact is minted from `look` of the donor file; that is guidance about which observation to select from, not a new rule, since the relation is indifferent to which kind produced the bytes. Weaker relations fail: per-line containment lets an author stitch non-adjacent lines into a sentence the donor never wrote, and whitespace- or case-normalised matching means the memo shows text the capture does not contain — both are paraphrase with extra steps.

rows.text: Containment against a fact's whole output has one genuine unsoundness, and it is fixable by the same schema move TET-28 already made. Fact.output is built at mint by joining the buffer entries' non-empty outputs with "\n", and the per-entry boundaries are not stored — so "substring of fact.output" can be satisfied by text straddling the seam between two observations: bytes that were never contiguous in anything the author actually saw, e.g. the tail of one file's capture concatenated with the head of another's. The fix is a serde-defaulted per-entry field on ExtentEntry recording the entry's output byte length, mirroring exactly how kind and pattern were added for TET-28: boundaries become reconstructible from lengths (skipping zero-length entries, matching the mint-time filter), the premise relation is then "verbatim substring of a single observation's output", and a donor fact minted before the field existed is ineligible with the same remedy TET-28 gives legacy facts — re-look and re-mint. Absent means not recorded, never guessed.

rows.text: The transplant record's shape follows from precedents already shipped, one field at a time. A transplant is an append-only record declared by a new verb (one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, one new Kind variant and counter): (a) the donor is a citation of exactly ONE fact — the same single-citation rationale targets.rs states ("a target resting on 'one of these several facts' would leave which one undecided"), and a fact citation rather than a typed path because the donor site is then the fact's captured extent, which no author can type; (b) premise rows are verbatim selections from that donor fact's output (per C3-C5), immutable once selected — a selection of immutable bytes has nothing to revise honestly — and withdrawable with --why, mirroring target's withdraw-not-revise discipline; (c) a premise is discharged by citing a claim, in a separate later act, and because `tetel claim` refuses without --cites and on unknown fact ids, a discharge claim rests on at least one real fact by construction — the ticket's "must that claim itself rest on a fact?" is answered yes with zero new machinery; (d) a discharge can be superseded by a later discharge citing a different claim, append-only, so a refuted-and-replaced claim does not strand its premise.

rows.text: The transplant's destination should be a citation of a live modification target (T#), not a typed path and not an independent record — the two features compose. A transplant installs the donor's mechanism at a site the design necessarily tells the implementer to modify, so under TET-28's own rule that site should already be a declared target; making the transplant verb refuse a destination that is not a live target turns one declaration into a forcing function for the other, and narrows TET-28's admitted under-declaration blind spot for exactly the fix-shape that produced the motivating defect. The composition costs nothing at the edge cases: a green-field destination (new code, new symbol) is still censusable, because censuses() deliberately accepts a NoMatch search — "a symbol with no occurrences is censused by the grep that established it has none" — so declaring a target for a symbol that does not exist yet works today; and the destination-holds claims get a named, censused destination instead of a prose phrase. What the tool cannot verify — that the cited target really is where the mechanism lands — is content, and stays printed as non-coverage rather than guessed at.

rows.text: An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. Refusing a premise row that cites no claim at declaration time would demand the destination-holds claim exist before the premise can be recorded, inverting that order (answer first, transcribe after) and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward not declaring it at all — the same "refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one" failure scope.rs's discriminator names. TET-28 never faced this because a census either exists or does not; a premise inventory is built across time. So the workspace invariant enforced at the verb is only "every premise is a genuine quotation of the cited donor's capture" (plus: donor fact exists and carries span boundaries, destination target exists and is live, a discharge cites an existing live claim); "every premise is discharged" is not a workspace invariant at all — it is a property of the finished document.

rows.text: The refusals land on three surfaces, each the earliest that can decide its own question. (1) At the verb: quotation invariants — donor fact exists and is span-eligible, premise text is a verbatim substring of a single observation's output, destination is a live target, a discharge names an existing live claim. These are per-record and decidable at creation, exactly like target's census refusal. (2) At `render --out`: completeness — a live transplant with an undischarged premise (none cited, or its discharge claim withdrawn) refuses the write. This is deliberately later than the verb (the intermediate state is legal while authoring) and deliberately earlier than check (the ticket's placement): --out is the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot under the pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited, so a memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise should fail to come into existence rather than exist and fail; the remedy is singular — discharge the premise, or withdraw it or its transplant with --why. A preview render (no --out) still assembles, marking undischarged rows loudly, so mid-work visibility is preserved; this render/--out asymmetry is new, and it is the design's most debatable departure. (3) At check: re-verification of everything above against the shipped snapshot — both directions, since tampering can go either way (a transplant row the snapshot lacks; a snapshot premise whose text is not contained in its donor fact's output; a premise whose discharge claim is withdrawn or missing) — as a machine failure in the same partition as uncensused targets, with rows in a snapshotless document reported human-owed as unverifiable, the standing choice for snapshot-dependent findings. Containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from facts.jsonl, which already ships full outputs; check runs nothing and fetches nothing to do it.

rows.text: The containment relation was tested against the motivating case itself, at the source, and it passes — with one correction to the ticket's framing. The missed premise ("its parent is remote-known or was walked earlier in this same session", remote_utils.rs:4576 in lonic-forklift at HEAD) is contiguous bytes in a raw capture of the donor file, both as a single clause within one line and as the full seven-line `//` comment with its prefixes, so the verbatim-substring refusal admits it without any comment-syntax knowledge. But the premise does NOT live in the donor function's `///` doc block — collect_changed_closure's doc block never states the insert-before-check discipline or its ordering premise; both live only in the body comment below the signature. So the ticket's phrase "the donor's comment-stated premises" must not be operationalised as "the donor's doc block": the relation has to range over whatever bytes the author captured of the donor site, and a premise stated at a call site or in a body comment is selectable exactly when the author's donor fact folded an observation that covers it — the relation thereby pressures the author to capture the donor widely enough, and a known-but-uncaptured premise demands another look, not a typed row. Separately, today's repaired destination twin states the once-missed condition as one gradeable sentence ("Sound only parents-first — a child that marked a parent-explained hash would otherwise short-circuit the explaining parent's own audit"), which is concrete evidence that the discharge obligation this design demands — one claim per premise, stating that it holds at the destination — fits in a single claim proposition for the hardest observed case.

rows.text: The rendered section follows compose.rs's shipped conventions with one deliberate difference. A "## Transplants" section renders beside the modification-target section: per live transplant, the donor fact id with its extent labels (labels, never absolute keys — the committed-document rule), the destination target id and symbol, and one entry per live premise carrying the selected text verbatim in a fenced block with the discharging claim id beside it; withdrawn transplants and premises are dropped, and once any claim exists the section renders even when empty ("none declared"), because the hole is the finding — the same visibility answer to under-declaration the target section shipped. The deliberate difference: compose.rs refuses to inline captured output into the document because output is unbounded, but a premise is an author-bounded selection, not a whole capture, so inlining it verbatim is both safe and the entire point — the reader must see the donor's clause on the page, spelled the way the donor's file spells it, or the section is a list of opaque pointers. Fenced blocks rather than table cells because a premise legitimately spans lines and markdown table cells cannot carry multi-line verbatim text without escaping, which would violate byte-fidelity.

rows.text: What the mechanism cannot catch is boundable and belongs in check's printed NON_COVERAGE list, which exists for exactly this ("a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed"). Six entries: (a) a transplant the author never declared — no refusal can reach it; the empty section is its only trace; (b) premises the donor never wrote down — the relation selects from captured text, so a premise that lives in the donor's structure rather than its comments has nothing to select; (c) premises outside the captured extent — a donor fact that folded too narrow a look cannot yield a premise from the lines it never captured; (d) shallow selection — the tool verifies that selected bytes are the donor's, never that they are all the load-bearing ones; selecting one convenient clause and stopping is invisible to any format-level check, because deciding what counts as a premise is design judgment (the ticket says so) and deciding a selection is too small is a truth-check, the insincere-examination ceiling this project registered as permanently out of reach; (e) whether the discharge claim actually addresses its premise, and whether the cited target really is the mechanism's destination — both content; the claim is graded by a grounding pass as written, and the linkage is graded by nobody; (f) a donor comment that is itself wrong — verbatim quotation establishes provenance, never truth. None of these is reachable by a format-level refusal, so printing them is the honest disposition, not a fallback.

rows.text: The mechanism's value is precisely that it moves one property across check's oldest declared blind spot, and grounding then does the rest. Per the ticket's account of the FORK-94 trail — recorded here as the ticket's report, not re-established — the defective remedy was graded supports twice, correctly, because the violated property was asserted by no claim at all; that situation is exactly the first entry in check's standing non-coverage list, "dependents that never declared themselves", and a grounder that grades propositions as written has nothing to grade where there is no proposition. Every piece of this design funnels toward converting that absent proposition into a present one: the premise row forces the donor's condition onto the page as captured bytes, and the discharge obligation forces a claim that the condition holds at the destination — a claim like any other, resting on facts by construction, entering the evidence ledger, graded by the next grounding pass, revisable and then out-of-proof until regraded. The tool never judges whether the claim is true; it refuses only the shape in which the question goes unasked. And the hardest observed case shows the converted claim fits in one sentence: today's repaired destination states the once-missed condition in a single doc-comment sentence, first-hand evidence that the discharge obligation is one gradeable proposition, not an essay.

rows.text: The ticket's anchor — "revised since the last grounding pass" — would have gone silent on the finding the ticket cites. `brief::build` returns every ledger claim unconditionally, including already-grounded ones ("A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on"), so every subsequent pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed and appends records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest. This is measured, not inferred: in the two shipped memos, tet28's C9 carries ten records on one unchanged digest from three passes spanning 1690 seconds, and tet28's C13 was graded `qualifies` by two passes 918 seconds apart on unchanged text. So an anchor at the *latest* grading advances past any fix-round prose edit as soon as one more pass runs — and the FORK-94 trail the ticket describes ran six rounds. The anchor must instead be the *earliest* record grading the claim's current wording: the moment that wording first entered proof, which a later pass over unchanged text cannot move.

rows.text: The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) every id it cites resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger, (c) every one of those claims is in proof under the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of the claim's current proposition, with the empty digest grandfathered — and (d) the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text is strictly greater than the maximum, over its cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Clause (d) settles the ticket's two ambiguities together: the per-claim anchor is the earliest record grading the current wording, and the per-block anchor is the latest of those, so a block is listed only once its whole evidence base has settled and its text has moved since. Run against the two shipped memos it lists nothing: tet28's and tet29's post-grounding prose revisions each accompanied a claim revision, so the new wording's first proof postdates the edit, and tet28's six post-grounding revisions that did not are heading blocks. Given a FORK-94-shaped edit — tet29's P11 moved 600 seconds past the last first proof with no claim touched — it lists exactly that block and nothing else, and giving one of its cited claims a later first proof clears it.

rows.text: The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.

rows.text: This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.

rows.text: There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block — not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` — and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render — falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. The timestamp comparison resolves exactly that ordering, which is why it is worth its stated bound.

rows.text: The vacuous cases are excluded by the in-proof gate rather than by a special case, and the exclusion is justified by non-overlap: a claim with no records at all is already printed as `ungrounded`, and a claim whose every record grades superseded text is already a machine failure as `out_of_proof`, so a prose block resting on either is already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof therefore makes a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo mid-first-draft, list nothing at all — the residue is empty until a memo has been graded, which is when it starts being able to say anything. Two populations fall outside the rule and are worth naming rather than counting: heading blocks, and paragraphs that cite nothing. A paragraph with no citation is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare against, so its invisibility here is a real gap and belongs in the printed non-coverage list, not in a footnote.

rows.text: The residue is bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, not a new section, and it is identified by document line as well as by block id. The partition has no sub-headings — it is one list of `  - ` entries, some of which already run to several indented lines, as `mint_windows` and `tree_states` do — so a section would be the only one there and would say by its shape that it outranks the rest. One entry per listed block, plus a single preamble entry carrying what is constant across them: that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same. Printing that constant once rather than in every bullet follows the precedent this crate set when `no scope declared` was collapsed to one document-level line, on the stated grounds that repeating a constant per row "buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant". The entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because `compose::render` never writes a block's id into the output and an id alone names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find; the offsets come from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render` so that the block-to-line mapping is described in exactly one place. It also names each cited claim, that claim's first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, so a reader can disbelieve the conclusion.

rows.text: Declaring this design's own modification targets took six whole-worktree searches — `check_file`, `prose_after_proof` and `block_offsets` in one fact, `Findings`, `NON_COVERAGE` and `render` in another — and measured a cost of the census mechanism that compounds with each memo the repository accumulates. A census is a whole-worktree search whose entire output is captured into a fact and shipped in the snapshot; in this repository the two previous memos' snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines, up to 57110 bytes each, so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. The measured weight for the four of the six symbols that already exist: `render` 486 matching lines and 405019 characters, `NON_COVERAGE` 35 lines and 98828 characters, `Findings` 23 lines and 59.2 KB, `check_file` 5 lines and 285 bytes; the two green-field symbols have no occurrences at all and are censused by the searches that established that. Two consequences follow. The largest captures exceeded what the authoring surface would return, so those symbol populations were established by the search while their individual sites went unread by the author — the census establishes rooting and extent, never that anyone looked at each site, which is a thing the census's own printed non-coverage already says in a different form. And the cost grows: every memo added to `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of any symbol it discusses.

rows.text: The contract TET-42 should adopt, per artifact: (1) a rendered memo guarantees that every tool-generated extent label citing a file inside the worktree the observation was taken against is spelled relative to that worktree root, and makes no promise about author-typed text or about `proc:` command lines; (2) an evidence ledger inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]` and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because it is the identity of the tree, not a citation into it; (3) a snapshot keeps every `key` absolute and canonical, because `key` is what `ExtentEntry::censuses` compares against `world_root`, and stores the same relativized labels the memo renders. rows.text: The explicit-path exception must be implemented as a decision about whether to pass exclusion flags at all, and `look_grep`'s existing shape already supplies the discriminator. `look_grep` adds `-r` only when `root_path.is_dir()`, and passes `root` through to grep verbatim as the caller spelled it, never canonicalized. So the rule is: when the root is not a directory the caller has named a single file explicitly, and no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude` otherwise suppresses a file named on the command line. When the root is a directory that is itself tetel content, again no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude-dir` otherwise suppresses a directory named as the recursion root. A root counts as tetel content by three format tests and no others: some component of it ends with the literal `.tetel`, or its filename ends with `.evidence.jsonl`, or a directory named by appending `.tetel` to it exists. Only in the remaining case, a directory root that is not itself tetel content, are the three exclusions passed, and each must be spelled the way grep will construct the matched file's name from that same root string.

rows.text: The ticket's headline reframing — that census output cost "~135k tokens, roughly 40% of the designer's reported 336k run" — is not reproducible from this design's evidence, and this run produced a direct counter-instance rather than merely failing to confirm it. `look_grep`'s return is genuinely uncapped in tetel: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` copies the grep's whole stdout into what `LookOutcome` hands back, with no length check, truncation or configuration between them. But when this design took a real whole-worktree census, the client harness rejected the 707,751-character result and returned roughly 1,300 characters of error text naming a spill file instead. So a large census's bytes need not enter a model's context at all, and the uncapped return does not by itself establish any figure in tokens. Two things remain true and are worth more than the figure: the bound that fired belongs to the caller rather than to tetel, and a different caller will not supply one; and nothing in `look_grep` records that anything downstream bounded what it returned, so a truncation leaves no trace in the fact it was minted into.

rows.text: Supersession needs no verb and withdrawal needs one, and both are resolved by log order rather than by timestamp. Supersession is automatic: since suppression is existential over matching keys, a later ack with a different key simply fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing. Withdrawal is a second event, `Unack`, carrying a block id and its own required verbatim `--why`; suppression then requires a key-matching ack appended after the last `Unack` for that block. Naming only the block, rather than a key, is sufficient because a key-mismatched ack is already void. Resolving by position in an append-only log written one line per event, rather than by comparing timestamps, keeps the whole acknowledgement mechanism free of clock comparisons. Withdrawal has to exist: without it, an author who acknowledged in error and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would have no honest act available — which is precisely the defect this design was written to remove, reproduced one level up.

rows.text: This design knowingly breaks both halves of TET-30's C11 sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes": a tenth file ships, and a new event schema exists. The price is bounded and should be stated rather than absorbed. `check` always prints the binary that produced a report, on the stated ground that a report which does not name its build cannot be disbelieved, so two reports disagreeing about one memo's residue can be attributed to their checkers — which is sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses. It is not sufficient to tell the reader of a single old report that an acknowledgement exists at all; what covers that is the acknowledgement log itself, which the snapshot ships beside the memo and which is readable without any tetel build.

rows.text: Two entries are owed in `NON_COVERAGE`, by the list's own stated standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed. First: that an acknowledgement records only that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and that nothing verifies the reading happened or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — the tool's silence after an ack is the author's assertion, not the tool's finding. Second: that an acknowledgement minted after the last `render --out` is not in the snapshot the check reads, so it does not suppress anything until the memo is re-rendered. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.

rows.text: Per-citation attribution is folded into the acknowledgement only as far as it honestly can be, which is not far. `NON_COVERAGE`'s last entry already states that whether a block's wording was ever examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is never answered by any listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it either: the ack is per block, its key merely records every cited claim's digest, and the only place a per-citation judgement can appear is inside the author's verbatim `--why`, which the tool must not parse. rows.text: The acknowledgement log is re-homeable into TET-36's obligation ledger without rewriting a single event, because no field in it is specific to this residue. It records a block id, the block's text and citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp; it records none of the quantities `prose_after_proof` derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not whether the block was listed. A general ledger consuming these as discharge records for one obligation class therefore needs the events as they stand and a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing rather than a rework.
